tip.title: Climb stairs hard for one minute, three times a day
tip.why: You do not need a workout to get most of what a workout gives you; you need a few moments of being out of breath. In the UK Biobank, Stamatakis and colleagues (Nature Medicine, 2022) followed 25,241 adults with an average age of 62 who said they did no exercise in their leisure time, but who wore a wrist accelerometer for a week. The device picked up what they called vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity, or VILPA: bursts of a minute or two, such as taking the stairs fast, carrying heavy shopping or hurrying for a bus. Over about seven years of follow-up, people with the median amount, around 4.4 minutes a day spread over roughly three bouts, had 26% to 30% lower all-cause and cancer mortality and 32% to 34% lower cardiovascular mortality than people with none. It is observational, so part of the gap is that healthier people move harder, but a separate analysis of regular exercisers found the same pattern, and the dose that mattered is small enough to hide inside a normal day.
how: Pick three stairwells or hills you already pass today and take each one fast enough that you could not hold a conversation at the top; 60 to 90 seconds is plenty.
If there are no stairs, walk the last two blocks to lunch at a pace that feels slightly silly, or carry the heavy grocery bags in one trip.
Count bouts, not minutes: three short bursts you actually do beat a gym session you keep postponing.
tip.ask: Which three moments in your day could turn into a one-minute burst, and did the first one leave you out of breath?

markets.headline: Stocks fell broadly Monday as chipmakers sold off ahead of Nvidia's Tuesday report, with the S&P 500 down 1.9% to 7,416.59 and the Nasdaq off 2.5%.
points: The S&P 500 lost 145.08 points (1.92%) to 7,416.59, the Dow fell 739.38 points (1.41%) to 51,608.17, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.49% to 24,509.76, its third straight decline. Semiconductors did the damage: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell more than 5% with every member lower, and Yahoo Finance estimated the chip group shed over $400 billion in value in one session even though roughly 7 in 10 S&P 500 stocks rose. Nvidia closed at $156.14, down 4.12%, its lowest since July 2025, as the Commerce Department tightened rules on overseas access to advanced AI chips and at least five firms cut their Nvidia price targets (UBS to $240 from $300) while keeping Buy ratings. Asian chip shares had sold off overnight, and the Anthropic IPO later this week added to the focus on AI valuations.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh opened a San Francisco Fed conference Monday with prepared remarks laying out three AI scenarios, including one in which AI investment returns disappoint, equity valuations fall and unemployment rises; he called them illustrative scenarios, not forecasts, and the selloff was under way before he spoke. Treasuries caught a small bid: the 10-year yield slipped more than 2 basis points to about 5.13% after touching 5.174% Friday, its highest in years, following last week's hot producer-price data; markets still price a December rate hike. Tuesday's set-up: Home Depot reports before the open (consensus EPS $3.84 on about $42.8 billion revenue), and Nvidia reports after the close, with Wall Street looking for EPS of about $2.47 on revenue near $108.8 billion in the first report hosted by interim CEO Colette Kress since Jensen Huang's resignation. Palo Alto Networks follows Wednesday after the close.

Tesla fell $10.48 (2.69%) to $379.74, giving back part of last week's gains. Reports said an all-stock acquisition of Tesla by SpaceX is now the likeliest outcome of the merger talks, with an announcement possible as early as December; no terms or filing have been disclosed, and the stock traded lower on the dilution and structure uncertainty. Separately, Tesla opened Cybercab purchases to select customers at $29,990 plus a $299 monthly subscription and extended Cybertruck production; Barclays' Dan Levy said the recent robotaxi and Cybercab updates support the robotaxi narrative, though the note did not stop the slide.

Intel dropped $4.19 (7.02%) to $55.47, far worse than the Nasdaq. A proposed shareholder class action filed Friday in federal court in San Jose names Intel, CEO Lip-Bu Tan and the CFO, covers holders from July 23 to October 29, and alleges the company concealed weak PC demand before the roughly 29% one-day plunge after its late-October report; the broader chip selloff ahead of Nvidia was the other pressure. After the close Intel fell a further 3.6% to about $53.46 when a filing showed Nvidia cut its Intel stake by 25% in the third quarter. SpaceX slipped $1.75 (1.26%) to $137.36 despite a wave of positive notes after Starship Flight 15, which caught the upper stage for the first time but lost the Super Heavy booster: Citi raised its target to $280 from $240 (Buy), Raymond James reiterated Strong Buy with an $800 target, Goldman kept Buy at $245, and Wells Fargo ($274), RBC ($225), Bernstein ($268) and Pivotal ($260) reiterated positive ratings; TipRanks shows a Strong Buy consensus (28 Buy, 5 Hold, 1 Sell) with a $267.76 average target.

pick.name: Keysight Technologies
pick.theme: Test-and-measurement supplier to the AI data center and wireless buildout, reporting Thursday after a 27% pullback from its October high
pick.what: Keysight Technologies, based in Santa Rosa, California, makes electronic design, test and measurement equipment and software: oscilloscopes, network and signal analyzers, signal generators, and simulation and network-test tools, including the Ixia and Spirent network-test businesses. Its customers are chipmakers, networking and data center equipment vendors, wireless carriers, automakers and aerospace and defense contractors who need to validate high-speed interconnects (such as 1.6T Ethernet and 224G links), 5G and early 6G radios, and power electronics. It reports in two segments, Communications Solutions and Electronic Industrial Solutions, with a large recurring software and services base. The fiscal year ends October 31, so Thursday's report covers the fourth quarter and sets guidance for fiscal 2027.
pick.why: KEYS closed Monday, November 16, at $285.63, down 4.05% in the chip-led selloff, about 27% below its all-time intraday high of $389.93 set October 6 and up from a November 5 closing low of $260.61. The company reports fiscal fourth-quarter results Thursday, November 19, after the close; Earnings Whispers shows consensus of about $3.09 EPS on $1.94 billion revenue (MarketBeat's figure is $3.37 on $1.95 billion), and Keysight has beaten the consensus in six of its last seven quarters by an average of about 11%. Analysts have stayed constructive through the drawdown: StockAnalysis shows a Buy consensus from 12 analysts with a $419.67 average target, MarketBeat shows Moderate Buy at $401.42, and Citi ($400) and Morgan Stanley ($425) reiterated Buy on November 12. The stock fell 8.7% on October 22 and another 9% on November 5 as AI-infrastructure names were de-rated, so the setup is a test-equipment name whose AI and 1.6T data center demand story is intact on paper but whose multiple has been cut ahead of a print that will show whether orders held up. An idea to research, not a recommendation.
pick.risk: Keysight is tied to capital spending by the same AI, networking and semiconductor customers that are selling off now, and Nvidia's Tuesday report and guidance could swing the whole group before Keysight prints. Earnings expectations differ by source ($3.09 to $3.37 EPS), so a result that beats one bar can miss another, and weak fiscal 2027 guidance would likely overwhelm a fourth-quarter beat. The shares have already fallen roughly 27% in six weeks and remain volatile, with multiple 8%-plus single-day drops since October.

btc.summary: Cowen's newest video, posted Monday morning and titled Bitcoin: Dubious Speculation, is his short-term read of a market sitting at three-month lows, and crypto outlets summarizing his latest commentary Monday put the emphasis on the calendar. He lines November and December up against the same stretch in past rate-hike cycles and calls them the critical months: in his view the bear market may be nearing its end in time, but that does not rule out one more price low, with late December the likeliest moment for the final flush. He expects a short-lived rebound could come first and warns against treating a bounce as the bottom; the level he keeps pointing to is the realized price, the average cost basis of all coins, which earlier bear markets dipped below before turning. His practical stance is unchanged from last week: keep dollar-cost averaging rather than trying to call the exact low.

articles.title: XPeng dates its IRON humanoid ramp to January 1, 2027
body: XPeng used its third-quarter earnings call on Monday, Nov. 16 to put a calendar date on its IRON humanoid. Benzinga reported that CEO He Xiaopeng said **mass production starts Jan. 1, 2027**, with an external commercial launch in the second quarter of 2027, and that he expects the robot could eventually outsell the industry's hottest premium EVs. XPeng's US-listed shares rose about 6% on the day.

The robot news arrived wrapped in mixed car results. Revenue was 24.28 billion yuan, up 19.1% from a year earlier and ahead of the roughly 23.2 billion yuan analysts expected, on 118,390 deliveries, according to the call transcript. Gross margin slipped to 18.9% from 20.1%, and the net loss widened to 0.87 billion yuan from 0.38 billion, so the humanoid program is being funded by a car business that is still losing money.

For context, IRON walked off a newly commissioned Guangzhou line on Sept. 8. XPeng says the line is more than 80% automated and is aimed at about 1,000 units a month from the end of this year. The Jan. 1 date is the first time XPeng has pinned the ramp to a specific day rather than a quarter.

Two other Asia items landed Tuesday, Nov. 17. ROBOTERA said in a press release that its humanoids now work in **11 China Post hubs across eight cities in Guangdong**, which it calls the largest logistics deployment of embodied-intelligence robots so far. The program started at the Jianggao processing center in Guangzhou, where the robots were reported sorting up to 1,200 parcels an hour at a site that handles about 6.5 million mail pieces a day; ROBOTERA did not disclose how many robots are at each hub.

On the capital side, The National reported that Abu Dhabi's Lunate plans a humanoid-robot ETF that lists on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange on **Dec. 8 under the ticker ROBOTS**, initially holding 41 companies spanning semiconductors, robot components, humanoid developers and software. It gives Gulf investors a packaged way into the theme.

What it means: the commercial center of gravity for humanoids still sits in China, and the capital markets around it are getting more structured. For Western makers, a dated XPeng ramp and a China Post fleet that grows by hubs rather than by demos is the yardstick investors will hold against Figure, Agility and Tesla's 2027 timelines. Watch for XPeng's first unit count in January and whether ROBOTERA publishes per-hub robot numbers.

articles.title: Nvidia board shuts door on Huang return as chip stocks slide
body: Nvidia's board is not weighing a return by Jensen Huang as chief executive, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday, and Reuters cited three people saying the same; the directors are focused on the national-security investigation into him. That puts the board against a campaign backed by Elon Musk and endorsed by President Trump, who said he would welcome Huang back; an online petition had passed **180,000 signatures** by Monday. Huang resigned on Nov. 12 after 33 years running the company, leaving CFO Colette Kress as interim chief.

The same day the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule on remote access to advanced semiconductors. It adds license requirements for shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, and requires a license when an exporter knows chips are headed to a data center that would give a covered customer more than 12 million aggregate TPP, a measure of processing performance. The stated aim is to stop Chinese firms from renting restricted hardware through third-country clouds. Existing operators get 90 days to apply, and the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule is formally rescinded.

Chip stocks sold off. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 5.28%, Nvidia lost 4.12% to **$156.14**, its lowest close since July 2025, and AMD, Micron and Intel dropped about 5.6%, 7.6% and 7.0%. The Nasdaq Composite ended down 2.49% at 24,509.76 and the S&P 500 fell 1.92% to 7,416.59, its biggest drop since Nov. 5.

In San Francisco, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh opened the first hearing of the Fed's Productivity and Jobs Task Force by describing three scenarios staff are modeling: a productivity boom whose gains are shared, strong growth paired with automation-driven job losses, and an investment bust in which returns on AI spending disappoint, equity valuations fall and unemployment rises more sharply. "These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts," he said, according to CNBC. He did not discuss the December rate decision. Treasury yields slipped, with the 10-year near 5.13%, and futures still priced about a **91% chance of a quarter-point hike on Dec. 9**.

What comes next: Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday at about 1:20 PM PT with the call at 2 PM, Kress's first as interim CEO; consensus is roughly $109 billion in revenue and $2.48 to $2.49 a share. An employee all-hands is scheduled for Wednesday at noon ET, the same day Anthropic prices its IPO, where the filed $70 to $78 range was unchanged as of Monday despite the FT reporting that bankers are weighing a price above it.

articles.title: Tesla commits 3 billion euros to build Cybercab at Giga Berlin
body: Tesla will spend about **3 billion euros (roughly $3.3 billion)** on a new Cybercab production building at Giga Berlin in Grünheide, plant manager André Thierig announced Monday, Nov. 16, with output targeted to begin in 2029. Tesla plans to file its permit application by the end of 2026 and start construction in the first half of 2027, Electrek and Tesla North reported.

Thierig called the sum a first step and said the site could eventually build as many as 1 million Cybercabs a year, taking Tesla's total investment in Berlin and Brandenburg to about $10 billion. Electrek pointed out that EU rules currently cap driverless vehicles at 1,500 per model per year, and the announcement named no market or approval path for a car with no steering wheel or pedals.

The same day Electrek tallied the Cybercab's safety record: **eight crashes on file with NHTSA**. Four happened in driverless Robotaxi service and none exceeded 5 mph; the other four had a test driver aboard with driver assistance engaged, and one of those struck another car at 53 mph. The vehicle is being sold to invited buyers for $29,990 plus a required $299 monthly Autonomy Subscription, terms Bloomberg described Monday as steep even by Musk's own account.

Markets did not reward the factory news. TSLA fell 2.69% to $379.74 on Monday, a little worse than the Nasdaq's 2.5% drop, as chip stocks sold off ahead of Nvidia's report and as reports said an all-stock acquisition of Tesla by SpaceX is now the likeliest shape of the merger talks, with an announcement possible as early as December and no terms disclosed.

Berlin would give the Cybercab a second production base after Giga Texas, and the plan is a bet that European regulators will lift the 1,500-unit cap before 2029. The permit filing due by year-end should reveal the real floor area and phasing. Nearer term, the December delivery estimate for the first personal Cybercabs in Texas and the Dec. 3 shareholder meeting are the dates to watch.

articles.title: Alibaba ships Qwen4-Max, selling cost per task over raw scores
body: Alibaba released Qwen4-Max, the flagship of its fourth-generation model family. Release trackers date it Nov. 16 and one developer blog says it went live a day earlier, five days after a preview appeared on Alibaba's Token Plan. The company describes a mixture-of-experts model with a **2.4 trillion-parameter backbone and 71 billion active parameters per token**, a 1 million-token context window, text, image and video input, and reasoning switched on by default. The weights are not open.

The pitch is price rather than raw capability. API list pricing is **$1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens**, with cached input at $0.075, about 25% below the Qwen3.8-Max list. In a post on X, the Qwen team said token use on its internal Work360 agent evaluation fell roughly 24% to 35% compared with Qwen3.8-Max, and by about 48% to 49% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, cutting the average cost per Work360 task from $4.43 to $1.67.

Alibaba's own scores include 75.7 on DeepSWE v1.1, 48.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 51.7 on Humanity's Last Exam and a 1750 Elo on CodeArena; its own chart shows Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 well ahead on Terminal-Bench at 67.2. Independent measurements are cooler: Artificial Analysis gave it an Intelligence Index score of 43, ranking 38th of 81 models, while Vals AI scored it 63.2%, 11th of 38. VentureBeat called the result an uneven challenge to frontier rivals and noted that neither Alibaba's figure nor Artificial Analysis's own cost-per-task estimate ($3.27 versus $10.02 for Qwen3.8-Max, on a different workload) establishes a universal savings rate for customers.

Context: Alibaba previewed the Qwen 4 lineup (Max, Plus, Flash and a 27B model) at its Apsara conference on Sept. 22 without dates or prices, and commentators expect the smaller models to carry the open weights that self-hosters care about.

The takeaway: Chinese labs are now competing on the cost of completing an agent task rather than benchmark rank alone, and Alibaba is publishing token-efficiency numbers that invite independent checking. Whether the roughly 62% saving holds on customer workloads, and when the open-weight Qwen 4 models arrive, are the open questions.

articles.title: Ramon.Space raises $124 million as orbital compute money grows
body: Ramon.Space, a space computing company with roots in Israel, announced on Tuesday, Nov. 17 a **$124 million Series B led by growth equity firm PSG**, with Micron Technology, Senvest and Phoenix Financial joining earlier investors, Payload reported. The round takes the company's total funding to $180 million, and the company said the money will go to scaling production of its radiation-tolerant onboard computers to meet demand.

Ramon.Space's pitch is narrower than the Musk and Google visions. Its near-term business is processing satellite data in orbit rather than moving Earth's AI workloads into space, though it does plan to fly an orbital data center prototype in 2027 with Ingrasys, a Foxconn unit, under a partnership expanded in March.

The money is arriving as cautions grow louder. Axios reported Nov. 15 that researchers writing for the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum urged governments and companies to wait until collision, debris and military-targeting risks are better understood before putting data centers in orbit. The same piece cited Quilty Space: investment tied to orbital data centers has reached **$1.11 billion so far in 2026, up from about $197 million in 2025**, and Quilty's research director suggested companies are filing for more satellites than they will likely fly.

SpaceX stock slipped with the market. SPCX closed at $137.36 on Monday, down 1.26% as the Nasdaq fell about 2.5%, and sits roughly 39% below its 52-week high. On Starship, no FAA license for Flight 16 had been announced as of Nov. 16; the flight remains targeted no earlier than December from Launch Complex 39A in Florida, and Booster 23 still needs propellant loading and a static fire on the new pad.

What it means: private money is now flowing to the hardware layer that any orbital compute plan needs, which is also where near-term revenue exists, while the headline constellation filings remain far ahead of funded reality. The gap between $1.11 billion invested and a million-satellite application is what regulators and the Office of Space Commerce pilot will have to reconcile. Next markers: a Flight 16 license and pad tests at 39A, and whether Ramon.Space names its prototype's launch provider.

articles.title: Spot bitcoin ETFs snap outflow streak as IBIT turns positive
body: US spot bitcoin ETFs took in a net **$7.9 million on Monday**, ending a seven-session run of outflows, according to tallies based on Farside Investors data. The turn came almost entirely from BlackRock's IBIT, which drew $76.5 million and ended an 11-session outflow streak that had removed about $2.35 billion; the other funds lost a combined $68.6 million, with Grayscale's GBTC the largest at $34.6 million. The prior week's outflow was $1.07 billion, the third weekly loss in a row, and IBIT accounted for $908.4 million of it.

Prices stabilized rather than recovered. Bitcoin traded around $64,000 to $65,000 on Monday after the weekend slide to about **$62,000**, its sixth straight weekly decline, with the Fear and Greed Index still near 10 to 12, in extreme fear. Wintermute told CoinDesk the weekend's forced selling was not evidence of a bottom and that the bounce looked like short covering rather than new buying.

CoinDesk's markets desk framed Tuesday's Nvidia report as the near-term risk: a disappointment could trigger selling across risk assets and push bitcoin through support at $62,000 and then $60,000. CryptoQuant's Nick Pitto cautioned against reading much into a single day of IBIT inflows.

In Washington, the Senate Agriculture Committee holds a confirmation hearing Tuesday at 3 PM ET for CFTC nominees Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland; Chairman Michael Selig is currently the agency's only commissioner, and no committee vote has been scheduled, so it is unclear whether the Senate acts before January. The SEC nominees go before Senate Banking on Thursday.

What to watch: Monday's flows are one data point after two weeks of heavy redemptions, and whether IBIT's inflow repeats through Nvidia's results and Wednesday's FOMC minutes will say more than the headline. Futures still price a rate hike on Dec. 9, which has weighed on bitcoin all month.

articles.title: Centenarian gut enzyme signature improves metabolism in old mice
body: A UC San Diego team reported in Cell Metabolism on Monday that aged mice and human centenarians share a gut-microbiome signature: more microbial deconjugation of bile acids, carried out by the bacterial enzyme bile salt hydrolase (BSH). The human comparison drew on **125 centenarians, 107 older adults and 48 younger adults**. The authors propose that some age-related microbiome changes are protective adaptations rather than signs of decline.

To test that, they engineered a bacterium native to the gut to produce BSH continuously and gave a single dose to 82-week-old mice, roughly late middle age. The strain colonized stably and kept producing the enzyme; treated animals showed improved insulin sensitivity with supportive changes in body composition and modestly better glucose tolerance. The researchers stress that none of this shows the microbial change caused long life in humans, or that the engineered bacteria extend lifespan; they call the centenarian data corroborative, not definitive.

Fight Aging's Monday post revisited a Nature Biotechnology paper (published Sept. 7) in which Insilico Medicine and Vadim Gladyshev's lab applied six proteomic aging clocks to blood from a 12-week phase 2a trial of rentosertib, a TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Across 42 patients and 2,841 measured proteins, **all six clocks predicted lower biological age in treated groups than placebo**, by roughly three to four years on several clocks and up to six on one; the 30 mg twice-daily dose was most consistent, even though 60 mg once daily gave the bigger lung-function gain. Fight Aging's caveat: proteomic clocks cannot by themselves separate reversal of aging from relief of disease, and four of the five clock-development teams are co-authors.

Also this week, the Gerontological Society of America published a report, Unit of Health: The Currency of Longevity, on using wearable and electronic-health-record data as longevity indicators, while warning that precise personal forecasts could mislead or distress users and deepen health inequities.

Why it matters: the BSH work is one of the few microbiome-aging studies to move from correlation in centenarians to an engineered intervention in old animals, but the endpoint so far is metabolic health, not lifespan. The rentosertib analysis shows how aging clocks could ride along in ordinary drug trials, which is also why the conflict-of-interest and disease-confounding caveats matter.

vocab.def: A clumsy, inelegant fix that works anyway: a solution bolted together from mismatched parts because it had to ship today.

cards.b: Engineering slang popularized by Jackson Granholm's 1962 Datamation essay 'How to Design a Kludge'; often traced to German klug ('clever') or Scots cludgie, though the origin is disputed
hack, workaround, bodge, duct-tape fix, Rube Goldberg machine; the opposite of an elegant design
a zip-tied cable harness that shipped, the regex that parses a log file nobody will ever touch again, a hotfix with a TODO from 2023 still in it

examples: The gripper timing was a kludge, a 40-millisecond sleep nobody could explain, and it held through the whole demo.
Every lab has one kludge it is secretly proud of, and it is usually load-bearing.
vocab.ex: The gripper timing was a kludge, a 40-millisecond sleep nobody could explain, and it held through the whole demo.

vocab.def: Studied carelessness: the art of making something difficult look effortless, hiding all the work that went into it.

cards.b: Italian, coined by Baldassare Castiglione in The Book of the Courtier (1528) for the grace of a courtier who never seems to be trying
nonchalance, effortless grace, understated mastery; the opposite of visible strain or showing your work
a demo that looks easy because of three weeks of tuning, a chef plating without looking, an open-collar suit that took an hour

examples: The demo had real sprezzatura: the robot folded the shirt like an afterthought, and nobody saw the 400 failed runs behind it.
His slides have a kind of sprezzatura, four words a page and not a hint of the late nights that produced them.
vocab.ex: The demo had real sprezzatura: the robot folded the shirt like an afterthought, and nobody saw the 400 failed runs behind it.

vocab.def: A manuscript page that was scraped clean and written over, with traces of the old text still showing; by extension, anything that carries visible layers of its earlier versions.

cards.b: Greek palin ('again') + psēstos ('scraped'): parchment was expensive, so monks scraped off old texts and reused the skin
layered record, overwritten text, accretion; near relatives: patina, sediment, legacy code
a city block with 1920s brick behind a glass facade, a codebase where every refactor left fossils, a face that shows every earlier age

examples: The robot's control stack is a palimpsest: PID loops from 2019 still run under three generations of learned policies.
Downtown is a palimpsest of booms, with the cannery brick, the dot-com stucco and the new glass all on one block.
vocab.ex: The robot's control stack is a palimpsest: PID loops from 2019 still run under three generations of learned policies.

vocab.def: Relating to or living on the banks of a river or stream; the strip of land, plants and animals that depend on a waterway.

cards.b: Latin ripa ('riverbank'), the same root as the Spanish ribera and the French rive
riverside, streamside, bankside, littoral (for a lake or sea)
the willows along Stevens Creek, a wildlife corridor, the law of who owns a riverbank

examples: The riparian corridor along the creek was the only green line left on the map by August.
Water rights here are riparian: if your land touches the stream, you get a share of it.
vocab.ex: The riparian corridor along the creek was the only green line left on the map by August.

vocab.def: Glowing or flickering softly over a surface; of wit or light, playing lightly and brilliantly without heat.

cards.b: Latin lambere ('to lick'): a flame that licks across a surface without burning it
glowing, flickering, luminous, softly radiant
late sun on the bay, a gas flame on a stove, a friend's light and quick humor

examples: By 4:30 the lambent light off the salt ponds made even the parking lot look painted.
Her lambent wit kept the review going for two hours without anyone noticing the time.
vocab.ex: By 4:30 the lambent light off the salt ponds made even the parking lot look painted.

vocab.def: Casually unconcerned; carefree in a way that shows a light, almost careless lack of worry.

cards.b: French insouciant, from in- ('not') and soucier ('to care'), from Latin sollicitare ('to disturb')
nonchalant, carefree, breezy, unbothered
a surfer shrugging at a wipeout, a founder joking through a bad quarter, a cat on a warm car hood

examples: He gave an insouciant shrug when the demo robot fell over, and the room relaxed with him.
There's an insouciant charm to a city that closes its best street for a Sunday market.
vocab.ex: He gave an insouciant shrug when the demo robot fell over, and the room relaxed with him.

vocab.def: The tendency to see meaningful patterns or connections in random or unrelated data.

cards.b: Coined by German psychiatrist Klaus Conrad in 1958, from Greek apo- ('away from') and phainein ('to show')
patternicity, false pattern, seeing faces in clouds
a backtest that only looks predictive, a 'trend' in three data points, a conspiracy theory

examples: Three green days in a row isn't a signal; that's apophenia talking.
Robot logs invite apophenia: every glitch looks like a pattern until you count.
vocab.ex: Three green days in a row isn't a signal; that's apophenia talking.

spanish.phrase: Me voy a echar un coyotito
spanish.pron: meh voy ah eh-CHAR oon ko-yo-TEE-toh
spanish.meaning: I'm going to take a quick nap
spanish.note: Literally 'I'm going to throw myself a little coyote'. In Mexico, echarse un coyotito is the everyday way to say you are grabbing a short nap, usually after lunch or before going out. Warm and a bit playful, fine with coworkers and family alike, and it makes the nap sound like a plan instead of a lapse. The reflexive echarse ('to throw oneself') shows up all over casual Mexican Spanish for doing something quickly: echarse un taco, echarse una pestañita.

cards.es: Me voy a echar un coyotito, ¿me despiertas en veinte?
cards.en: I'm going to take a quick nap, wake me in twenty?

cards.es: Me eché una pestañita en el tren
cards.en: I dozed off for a bit on the train (literally 'a little eyelash')

cards.es: Ando que me caigo de sueño
cards.en: I'm so tired I could fall over

parts.en: I'm off, I'm going (irse, to leave)
to throw; here 'to have' or 'to take', as in echarse algo
little coyote (diminutive of coyote), slang for a short nap

dialog.es: ¿Vienes al café o qué?

dialog.es: Dame veinte minutos, me voy a echar un coyotito.
dialog.en: Give me twenty minutes, I'm going to take a quick nap.

dialog.es: ¿Otra vez? Anoche no dormiste, ¿verdad?
dialog.en: Again? You didn't sleep last night, did you?

dialog.es: Casi nada. Al rato te alcanzo.
dialog.en: Barely. I'll catch up with you in a bit.

spanish.use: Say it after lunch today when you feel yourself fading; it names the nap, gets a smile, and nobody argues with a coyotito.

spanish.meaning: I spaced out / I lost my train of thought
spanish.note: Literally 'the plane left on me'. In Mexico it is the standard way to say your mind wandered off: you missed what someone said, forgot what you were about to say, or drove past your exit. Friendly and self-deprecating, fine with anyone, and the perfect thing to say in a meeting when someone has to repeat the question.

cards.es: Perdón, se me fue el avión, ¿qué decías?
cards.en: Sorry, I spaced out, what were you saying?
Same idea: I lost the thread
I've got my head in the clouds today

parts.en: reflexive marker, makes it happen 'to itself'
to me (the one it happened to)
to zone out, lose your train of thought

dialog.en: Hey, so what do you think of the plan?

spanish.use: Say it the moment you realize you missed the last 30 seconds of a conversation today; it gets a laugh and a repeat, not an eye-roll.

spanish.meaning: It just clicked / now I get it
spanish.note: Literally 'the twenty just dropped on me'. Old Mexican payphones took a 20-centavo coin, and the call connected only when the coin dropped. So 'me cayó el veinte' is the moment the line goes live in your head: you finally understand something that had been sitting in front of you. Everyday, friendly, safe with anyone.

cards.en: Has it clicked for you yet?

cards.es: Hasta ahora me cae el veinte
cards.en: Only now is it sinking in

dialog.en: Ah! Now it clicks, that's why it came out negative.

dialog.es: Ves, a veces solo hace falta un cafecito.
dialog.en: See, sometimes all it takes is a little coffee.

spanish.use: Say it the moment a concept finally makes sense today, especially when it was hiding in plain sight; it tells the other person you were listening.

spanish.meaning: What a drag / I really can't be bothered
spanish.note: Hueva is literally fish roe, but in Mexico it means laziness or boredom. '¡Qué hueva!' is the groan you let out when something tedious lands on you: a rainy Sunday errand, a long meeting, a form. Among friends only; it is mildly crude, so skip it with your boss or your partner's parents.

cards.en: I can't be bothered / it bores me

dare.why: Your evening is spoken for and the rain holds off until late tonight, so this one lives in your lunch break. Walk to Red Rock Coffee on Castro Street, order whatever you like, open a notebook, put the pen on the page and lock your eyes on the cup and the hand around it. Draw the outline for five full minutes without looking down once, then do it a second time. The rule: eyes on the subject, never on the paper, and no erasing. The drawing will be wrong and alive, and that is the point.
dare.worth: Blind contour drawing is the oldest trick in art school for switching off the part of you that draws the symbol of a cup and switching on the part that sees the actual edges, and it works in one sitting. You walk back to work noticing shadows and curves you have skipped over for years.
dare.src: Kimon Nicolaides · The Natural Way to Draw (1941)
